scenes.text: Syllabus four point one, excerpt limiting friction and limiting equilibrium. the end, you can resolve forces along a slope. Find reaction and decide the friction. And calculate the downhill acceleration.

scenes.title: Picture the descent first

beats.text: Consider a block held on a rough slope. A rope pulls it uphill and slightly away from the surface.
The block is released. Despite the pull, it slides downhill and gains speed. The rope keeps pulling at the same angle as the block descends.
The block stays in contact with the slope. We will check why friction cannot hold it, then calculate its acceleration. Here is the whole question.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: Model the block as a particle of mass four kilograms, released from rest.
The rough plane is inclined at thirty degrees to the horizontal. Call this angle theta.
A constant pull P of eight newtons acts thirty degrees above the uphill direction of the plane. Call this second angle alpha.
The coefficient of friction is zero point two five. Take g as ten metres per second squared.
Contact is maintained. Only weight, the pull, normal reaction and friction act. Use the ideal friction model: while sliding, friction equals its limiting value.
Find the normal reaction, decide whether it slides, and find the actual friction and acceleration. We have all the information. Now resolve the forces.

scenes.title: Resolve weight and the angled pull

beats.text: Choose axes along the slope and perpendicular to it. Theta measures the slope from horizontal; alpha measures the pull from the slope.
Weight equals mass times g.
Four times ten gives forty newtons, vertically downwards.
Replace weight by its two components. The inward component is W cosine theta. The weight and inward normal enclose the slope angle.
Forty cosine thirty gives twenty root three newtons into the plane.
The downhill weight component is W sine theta.
Forty sine thirty gives twenty newtons downhill.
Now replace the pull by its components. The uphill component is P cosine alpha: adjacent to its angle.
Eight cosine thirty gives four root three newtons uphill.
The component away from the plane is P sine alpha: opposite its angle.
Eight sine thirty gives four newtons away from the plane.
These components replace the original weight and pull. We use each force once. The uphill component resists descent; the outward component reduces the surface support.

scenes.title: Perpendicular balance gives the reaction

beats.text: Contact with the straight plane is maintained, so perpendicular acceleration is zero. Reaction and the outward pull component balance the inward weight component.
Newton’s second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Taking away from the plane as positive, R plus V minus W perpendicular equals zero.
Substitute four for V and twenty root three for the inward weight component.
So R equals twenty root three minus four newtons. Keep this exact value for the friction calculation.
The reaction is positive, so contact is possible. The rope supplies some outward support. Reaction is therefore smaller than the inward component of weight.

scenes.title: Decide the motion before choosing friction

beats.text: At rest, friction adjusts up to its limit. Actual friction f is less than or equal to mu R.
The maximum friction is mu times the normal reaction.
Substitute zero point two five times twenty root three minus four.
This gives five root three minus one newtons.
Before friction, the downhill demand D is the downhill weight component minus the uphill pull component.
Twenty minus four root three newtons. Compare this demand with the friction limit.
The demand is approximately thirteen point zero seven newtons, greater than the maximum friction of seven point six six newtons.
Friction cannot maintain rest. The block slides downhill, so friction acts uphill. In our sliding model, actual friction is five root three minus one newtons.

scenes.title: The downhill resultant gives acceleration

beats.text: Take downhill as positive. The downhill weight component helps; the uphill pull component and friction oppose the motion.
Newton’s second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
The downhill weight component, minus H, minus f, equals m a.
Substitute twenty minus four root three, minus five root three minus one in brackets, equals four a.
Subtracting the bracket adds one and subtracts five root three. Collect terms: twenty one minus nine root three equals four a.
Divide both sides by the mass to get the exact acceleration.
The acceleration is approximately one point three five metres per second squared downhill.
With constant forces, acceleration stays constant. From rest, the block covers increasing distances in equal time intervals. The friction points uphill throughout the descent.

scenes.title: What if the pull follows the slope?

beats.text: What would change if the pull acted parallel to the plane instead? Would reaction still be reduced by the pull? Think about its perpendicular component.
A parallel pull has no perpendicular component. With contact maintained, reaction alone balances the inward component of weight.
So R equals m g cosine theta. That familiar formula works here because the pull contributes no outward support. The friction limit increases.
The uphill component also changes. Recheck the downhill demand against the new friction limit before deciding motion.
